canonical.name: The noncompact genericity statement is kept at residuality in the strong topology by design; the scaffold does not silently upgrade that claim to an unconditional open-dense theorem.

Compact openness is split into two load-bearing lemmas: persistence of the old nondegenerate critical points via a uniform Hessian gap, and exclusion of new critical points away from fixed critical neighborhoods by a positive lower bound for |df| on the compact complement.
The same compact openness split needs the no-new-critical-points half explicitly; persistence alone does not rule out fresh zeros of the perturbed differential elsewhere.

Distinct critical values are imposed separately from the Morse condition by local bump perturbations that alter function values while leaving first and second derivatives unchanged at the chosen critical points.
Excellent Morse functions are therefore treated as a separate compact open-dense refinement, not as a hidden convention inside the word Morse.

The compact existence corollary uses Whitney embedding plus generic height functions as the main route, while the generic squared-distance theorem is retained as an independent embedded-manifold existence model for examples and later geometry.

Proper Morse exhaustions on noncompact manifolds are built shell by shell from a proper smooth exhaustion, using locally finite relative perturbations whose sizes decay fast enough that escape to infinity still forces the function to grow.

The properness-preservation lemma is kept separate because it carries the only noncompact analytic bookkeeping: the perturbation is locally finite and smooth, but also quantitatively too small on each shell to destroy properness.
The noncompact warning is retained as its own remark so later pages cannot cite compact open-dense genericity without checking the compactness hypothesis.
Morse does not imply distinct critical values; excellence is the separate value-separation refinement.
The torus examples deliberately reuse the published four-critical-point height function to show both a generic Morse direction and the symmetric equal-critical-value failure of excellence.
The circle squared-distance example uses the center as the medial-axis failure and off-axis points as the generic Morse regime.
The value-separation example is the local bump-function realization of the excellent-function argument.
A compact Morse function can still have repeated critical values, with the standard torus height as the canonical witness.

The noncompact counterexample will use perturbations that are tiny on every fixed compact set yet create new far-out critical points, isolating exactly why compact-style openness fails without strong-topology control at infinity.
